issues.description: Field: SealSaloon.stock — The problem statement contains conflicting instructions about the SealSaloon.stock field. In one place (problem statement lines 70-71) it instructs students to declare a final instance field `stock` and initialize it in the instance constructor (i.e., an instance final Stock initialized in the constructor). Elsewhere in the same problem statement (lines 77-80) it explicitly requires the `stock` attribute to be static (shared across all instances). The solution implementation (SealSaloon.java) declares `private static final Stock stock = new Stock();`. This mismatch (instance-final vs static-final) is contradictory and prevents a single clear implementation approach for students.
issues.suggestedFix: Resolve the contradictory requirement for the `stock` attribute. Option A (preferred to match the solution): update the problem statement to state that `stock` is a static (class-level) field shared across all SealSaloon instances, and instruct students to initialize it at declaration or in a static initializer (not in the instance constructor). Option B: if the teaching intent is per-instance stock, remove the lines requiring `stock` to be static and keep the requirement to initialize a final instance `stock` in the constructor. Make the chosen design explicit in the problem statement and ensure the template/solution match that design.

issues.description: Method: SealSaloon.checkOrderReady — The UML/problem specification declares a no-argument method `checkOrderReady()` (signature: `+checkOrderReady(): void`) (problem statement UML line 32). The reference solution defines a different public signature `public void checkOrderReady(boolean enableLogging)` (solution SealSaloon.java, signature at line 20). This parameter mismatch means the solution's public API does not match the specification and could confuse students about the required method signature.
issues.suggestedFix: Align the public API with the problem specification. Either (A) modify the solution to provide a public no-argument `public void checkOrderReady()` that implements the described behavior (and, if logging control is needed, make an internal/private overloaded method `checkOrderReady(boolean enableLogging)`), or (B) update the problem statement and UML to declare `checkOrderReady(boolean enableLogging)` if the boolean parameter is intentional. Prefer adding a no-arg public method that delegates to the boolean variant so both the specification and any internal logging needs are satisfied.

issues.description: The problem statement defines a no-argument method checkOrderReady(): void (UML and textual description refer to checkOrderReady() with no parameters). The solution implementation declares a different signature: public void checkOrderReady(boolean enableLogging) and calls it from orderMeal as checkOrderReady(true). This mismatch means the same conceptual operation (serving ready orders) is referenced with two different method signatures: problem expects checkOrderReady() while the solution provides checkOrderReady(boolean). A student implementing the exercise according to the problem text would implement or look for a no-argument method, but the reference solution requires a boolean parameter and uses it to control logging. This inconsistency creates a mapping barrier and may confuse students about the required method signature and how to call it.
issues.suggestedFix: Align the method signature across artifacts. Preferred fix: change the solution to implement the no-argument method declared in the problem: public void checkOrderReady() { ... } and update the call in orderMeal to checkOrderReady(); remove or internalize any enableLogging parameter (e.g., use a private debug flag if logging is desired). Alternatively, update the problem statement to declare checkOrderReady(boolean enableLogging) and document the parameter and expected behavior, and ensure orderMeal calls checkOrderReady(true) consistently.
